grand_strategy.reading:
The United Kingdom runs the grand strategy of a power that has lost the
weight to act alone and the habit of not acting, and has decided to make
itself the organiser of the coalitions in which others' weight is added to its
own: the Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine with France, the JEF in the
north, bilateral treaties with Berlin, Warsaw, Paris, Oslo and Canberra, and
a nuclear role it now coordinates with Paris while it rents the delivery
system from Washington. Luttwak's reversal is everywhere. The more the UK
organises, the more it needs the American umbrella it is trying to insure
against; the more it obeys international law toward Washington (Iran bases,
Caribbean intelligence) the less Washington obliges it (Chagos, the Falklands
hints, tariffs); the more it engages China and the EU for growth, the more the
security and political price rises at home. Underneath is a politics
that has not found its centre: 2026 saw the May rout, Starmer's fall on
22 June and Burnham's arrival on 20 July with a poll bounce that Reform had
erased in YouGov's last September poll. Three signals that are not rows: the postponement of the
July UK-EU summit until Brussels knew who would be in Downing Street; the
Healey resignation that turned the 3% question into a government-wide problem;
and Washington's 'neutrality' statement on the Falklands only after a leaked
Pentagon email suggested otherwise. For the next review: whether a UK-EU summit
in November-December fixes the SPS and youth texts, whether the Autumn Budget
funds the Defence Investment Plan, and whether Burnham's 'all options' survives
contact with a Reform lead.
